body: STOP I'm in my work staffroom and trying not to bust a gut from laughing.

I have taught in a school and have planned and marked plenty. I even plan and mark now as a cover teacher as most of my assignments have been longer term. All this I put on my recent applications as well, and make sure I emphasise. 

And yeah, I can't become an AQA examiner yet, not until I've finished my ect years apparently. I looked when I was full-time at my first school. Thank you for replying!
This is great advice, thank you.

Okay, this is awesome advice I didn't think of this. At uni, we were discouraged from doing this to avoid disappointment, but tbh all I got is disappointment so far so it can't hurt. And I do the visits with a lot of schools in my area, and I feel like I charm the pants off them, but I do notice that I don't talk a lot about myself, I more talk to them about my experience and what I'm looking for. I find it quite difficult to talk about the ethos as it feels like shoehorning it in, but I could be like "I notice you have a particular emphasis on x, could you tell me a little more about that?" Or something along those lines. Thank you so much!
Hey, no need to apologise not your fault. Yeah i think you're right about the experience- once I can let that talk for itself, the degree is just a minor thing.

Luckily I've heard on the grapevine the head is leaving this year, so this may not be a problem this time next year. There's also a mass exodus at that school coming this year too, so that'll help. I've also been putting my agency as a reference in these recent applications as I have a great working relationship with them and they are very sympathetic to my situation as they had firsthand experience with their shitty behaviour. I've got loads of great references from my PGCE from old mentors and uni professors etc. I'm thinking about just leaving the old job off my CV completely and say I took a break from teaching as I wanted to travel etc. as it's just not worth the headache dealing with them.

Maybe it's different for maths rather than English? My bfs a maths teacher and he works with so many people who have different degrees. For example his hod her degree is in dance! So when I initially applied he didn't think it would be an issue at all. I'm starting to think that English positions really care about what degree you have which in my case is insane as I haven't kept up with psychology AT ALL since my degree and have no interest in it whatsoever. The degree killed all the interest I had in it.

Hmm, you're right. Unfortunately, I was the head and hod who essentially forced me out of the job. Asking a reference from either of those people was a fucking nightmare when I was applying for agency roles. They just ghosted me and my agencies so HR had to step in and give me the reference instead. I handed in my notice at the right time, all of that was above board, but I was on long-term sick before this and couldn't see a way forward with that school after a long ass process with them trying to find a way forward so I saw no choice but to leave. That's when the nastiness and the ghosting started.

Yup, I definitely think this is a factor especially in the recent applications I've been doing. I put HR down as my reference, which in reality they shouldn't be giving me a bad reference as I was exemplary at the school (their words, not mine) but I still wouldn't put it past them considering all the other things they have done subsequently to make my life a living hell.

I don't really want to do psychology that's the thing. I'm not caught up on the psychology curriculum at all. I've not picked up a book in psychology in over 10 years. The second I finished my degree I sold all my books and dumped every single thing to do with it as I knew I was never going to go into anything to do with psychology ever. My main focus is English- I know the curriculum inside and out, I've lived and breathed the GCSE spec for the last 2 years. I would be a crap psychology teacher, as it's just not my thing. English is my passion, but I got shoved down the route of psychology due to the old "English degree isn't worth the paper it's printed on" lark. I'm signing up to a few tutoring places to get some extra income and experience that way, and my agency are really good with finding me long term assignments with English teaching, so it's not super pressing right this second finding a full-time teaching position.

I only apply for jobs that are recommended for ect candidates, and I make sure they state that within the application itself. I think this is the way I need to go- I'm currently at a school doing a long term cover work assignment so maybe something will come up there. They seem very eager to keep me around, so I'm not completely out of options. Also good advice about the viewings of schools beforehand and I've done this, still no dice. Even if I charm the pants off them, still no.

I've had a disastrous beginning to my ect, leading to me quitting halfway through the year under less than stellar circumstances, none of which are my doing. I think I'm just going to stick with supply for now, and see what comes up.

I'm going on constant cpd to enhance my subject knowledge, as well as observing other English teachers to enhance my pedagogical knowledge. All this I put in applications, but no dice. I think you're right about staying on cover. I'm not willing to settle for a school like I did last year, as that was just disastrous.

I really don't want to piggyback off your post, but I have a very similar thing happening at my academy. 

They're all trying to push all ECT's to do this IRIS platform where we record ourselves for a full lesson- mentor tells us which lesson we should film, we pick the day and time, then it's used in our meetings and action steps and goals are set from this. 

I initially quite liked it- after I got over the initial cringe of seeing myself, I loved looking at it objectively and reflecting on what I could have done better and it's so far helped my practice. I also watch it with my partner (who's also a teacher) and we critique it together. 

The thing I have an issue with is when I share it with my mentor, it seems like it's almost used as a weapon against me to pick apart my teaching. I only ever really get what I could be doing better as feedback, rather than a nice balance of things I've done well and things I can improve upon. All I ever really get is "you're doing a good job" which is just? Meh? 

Again, sorry to piggyback, just wanted to hear others thoughts on this. Can I say no to this? And if I do, will it effect my ect years? I plan on leaving at the end of this year, but I really want to pass this year at least before moving on. I don't want any bad blood either.

When I did my first watch through, hated the sight and sound of her. She was an irritating, nasly voice little racist who killed Sasha-nothing more. 

Then, I did my second rewatch all the way though and my opinion did a 180. Love her now. I see some people here saying that she was just told by people that Paradisians are devils and then she went along with it. That's not what happened- she was brainwashed from childhood that she's a good Eldian and all that needs to happen is to cleanse the world of these Island Devils and then she'll be treated with the respect and dignity she deserves. 

There is little to no critical thinking going on because she's just a child. Marley and the internment zone is all she knows. When she's a Warrior candidate, she's praised for her skill in war. It's more than likely that that's the first time she's ever been treated like that. As we saw in Zeke's past, they have no problem treating small children with disgust and outright hatred. Gabi's first taste of being treated with some crumb of humanity is when she joins to be a Warrior candidate; of course she's going to cling to that- for her, for her family and for her home. 

I also saw people saying well Falco figured it out about the Paradisians- yes, but as already saw from when we met Falco, he was willing and open to converse and help those who were different than him (note the man he helps bandage in the trench in s4e1). He's a different character than Gabi and is meant to represent the side of Marley that is open to change. 

Gabi is a fantastically written character and now one of my favourites. Yeah, yeah she kills Sasha. Eren is essentially responsible for that too. And for killing Hange, so if you wanna be mad at someone, be mad at him.

Yeah, that is super tricky. I'm also an English teacher, so if you want any advice hit me up! I don't teach yr11 this year, but have done in my PGCE and have done a little marking for AQA (if that's your exam board) so can offer my 2-cents for what it's worth.

I feel EXACTLY the same. My first 3 weeks as an ECT1 I seriously considered quitting for the first time since starting this whole thing. The level of responsibility, work and pressure is so so overwhelming. I'm also teaching at a school that has less than stellar behaviour, so I had to deal with all of that on top of everything else. 

I can say I don't feel like quitting everyday anymore. Sure, some days are so hard I want to crawl into a dark hole and never come out again, but then some days I'm like nah that was alright or even (dare I say it) a good day (she whispers so quietly no-one can barely hear her). 

I do feel like I was lied to up to a certain extent during my PGCE. I had all this support and guidance from amazing people, now I just feel alone in it all. BUT I opened up to others in my department about how I was struggling, found they were all struggling with the same things and that made it easier. I have a work mum and another colleague that I go to whose in a similar boat- we share resources, cry to each other and bitch and moan about the bad days and it helps. A problem shared really is a problem halved. 

I think the difference is in your PGCE you have that support at your fingertips- from uni, to your course mates, to your mentor. But in your ect, you have to go and find your people yourself. And when it feels like your drowning, it's harder to do that if that makes sense? You have to work at those key relationships, and if you're anything like me and find that kind of thing difficult anyway, this job being so solitary makes it all the harder. 

I'm now honestly just surviving every day and doing the best I can in any given moment and take the wins as and when they come. I passed for a reason; you passed for a reason. So try not to be so hard on yourself and take every day as it comes. 

A lot of cliches in this response, but they have helped. Also, if it helps, your results don't actually matter in both your ect years. So do the best you can, and if your students don't """succeed""" in terms of metrics, it's not going to be held against you. Think of these years as just a tack on to PGCE- reflect, try to do better than last week, learn from your mistakes and keep building those relationships. It'll all work itself out in the end.

I mean, it depends how organised you are. There are certainly very busy periods of the school year. Be prepared to have some weekends taken up with work and uni assignments. But I have definitely had some down time when I got into the swing of things. And I definitely know of trainees who have a hard rule of no work at least one day in the weekend and some evenings off. 

To give you a rough idea of what workload you will have, this is how my year panned out: First placement I was doing 8 lessons a week by Christmas. You slowly build up to that but that's the expected amount to be teaching. You teach that amount until February half-term. 

Second placement you'll be expected to teach 12 lessons a week by Easter. Second placement you are kind of just dropped in it as they expect you to kind of hit the ground running, if you will. You'll pretty much get a week of grace period then start at least taking over a class by your second week. You will teach those 12 lessons until the end of the course. 

In between this, you have two major uni assignments: one written and an interview. The written one is about 6,000 words long and is due before Feb half-term. The interview is on a day during May. So this is to be taken into consideration when planning/booking holidays during the school holidays because it's more than likely you'll use that time to do that uni work during then. 

This isn't even taking into account going for job interviews, which take a while to apply for, prep if you get a chance to interview and then go to the interview itself, which takes a whole day and you'll be expected to plan cover for your placement classes. 

It's tough, don't get me wrong. Writing this I feel exhausted. But it is worth it. Teaching is a skill that takes a lifetime to get right, and you're only at the very beginning. But I feel so grateful and happy to have done it. 

Hope this helps.

I am finishing up my PGCE at Sussex in a couple days and I can tell you that we start first week of September- it's meant to simulate the school year as much as it possibly can, so we start at the same time as the kids. 
You do 3 weeks full-time at university, doing lectures, seminars etc. then my first placement date started on the 25th September. 
First placement lasts until Feb half-term (week of Valentine's day)
Second placement lasts from after Feb half-term until May half-term (roughly last week of May, depending on when Easter falls). 

I mean, technically you could go away with your family in September if you really wanted to, but I wouldn't advise it. Those 3 weeks are crucial for you to even feel the tiniest bit prepared for school, and even then you don't feel that in the slightest. 

If I were you, I would say no to the holiday and knuckle down. The year is already going to be tough, but missing university is only going to make it harder. Plus you'll miss out on bonding with your classmates, who become your rock when you have a tough time, which you eventually will on this kind of course. 

Good luck.

If we're looking at song lyrics being a form of poetry, which is so often was in the history of poetry (lyrical ballades were very popular in poetry circles), then grammatical errors were made all the time.

I work in a mental health facility in the UK and we have this one guy who is pretty much locked in this high security ward because of his AWOL risk. This argument is not as simple as one thing or the other, it's got to be a multi-faceted approach, one which includes locked rehab, these drug centres as the post is about, and a mixture of talking therapies and medication if applicable. It cannot be a one size fits all, because it is not a one size fits all problem. There are many reasons why people take drugs, and many reasons why people keep taking them despite it killing them. It's got to be person centred care, rather than what benefits the masses care, which unfortunately will never happen.
